speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: This is John Sarbanes with the view from inside and outside the nation's capital. Inside because I'm one of the members of Congress who's got an insider's perspective, but outside because I'm one of those who can come home every night and look back on Washington DC and kind of put it in perspective. Today I wanted to talk to you about what I call money drones. It's my phrase to refer to super PACs out there, and I've been talking a lot about money in politics. And I use that term money drones because if you're a candidate or a member of Congress and you're walking down the sidewalk, just running your campaign, suddenly you might hear a humming sound behind you. And next thing you know, one of these super PACs has dropped a half million dollar payload on your head of negative advertising. And that's the end of you politically. I was at a conference recently at Duke at the Sanford School of Public Policy and one of the students after I described these money drones actually asked a pretty insightful question. They didn't want to know about the effect on a campaign. They didn't want to really know about sort of the money equation so much. What they asked was how does it affect you mentally and emotionally if you're a member of Congress and you have to worry about these strikes from these money drones, from these super PACs coming in. It's a great question. You know, I'm one of the members of Congress who's in a district where I don't need to worry as much about one of these super PAC attacks, although frankly there's no member of Congress who can ignore them. So it maybe hasn't affected me directly in terms of agitating my mental and emotional state, but I can certainly say that there are colleagues of mine who face this kind of opposition this kind of onslaught every time they run their campaigns every two years and there's no question that it's affecting them it's no no question that it's affecting their their worldview it makes them nervous it makes them anxious makes them wonder whether they're going to be able to last in the job that they're trying to do and representing people so there there's something perverse about this new impact or influence of super PACs on our system and we have to do something about it. So I'm going to continue to talk about these issues and concerns but I wanted to mention in particular that question that I got from that student in North Carolina because I think she hit it right on the head when she raised that question. Again, this is John Sarbanes' view from inside and outside the nation's capital. I hope you'll continue to listen into our podcasts. If you want to learn more information about what we're doing to fight back against big money in politics, you can go to www.grastrootsdonor.com. And if you want to follow us on Twitter, our handle is at grassrootsdonor. Again, I look forward to hearing from you. With any questions you have, you can email us at grassrootsdonor.com and we hope you'll join our future podcast.

explicit_propositions.text: I am John Sarbanes, a member of Congress.
I will continue discussing issues related to money in politics.
I have both an insider's perspective and an outsider's perspective on Washington DC.
Super PACs are referred to by me as 'money drones'.
The website www.grastrootsdonor.com provides information about efforts to combat big money in politics.
There is a pervasive and harmful influence of super PACs on American democracy.
Money drones can deliver sudden, large-scale negative advertising payloads targeting candidates.
Some members of Congress experience anxiety and nervousness due to constant threats from super PACs.
A student at Duke University asked a meaningful question about the psychological effects of super PAC attacks on members of Congress.
The presence of super PACs distorts the political worldview of some legislators.

assumptions.text: Members of Congress should prioritize serving constituents over responding to external financial pressures.
The current structure of political financing allows for disproportionate influence by wealthy actors.
Emotional distress among lawmakers undermines effective democratic representation.
Political leaders have a duty to model integrity even when facing asymmetric pressure from dark money.
Trust in public institutions depends on transparency and accountability in campaign finance.
Public awareness of systemic corruption through media discourse is necessary for reform.
The student’s question reflects a deeper, underappreciated dimension of political dysfunction.
Audiences value personal narratives and moral appeals in political advocacy.
Legislators who lack exposure to super PAC attacks still bear responsibility for addressing systemic issues.
Online engagement platforms like websites and Twitter enhance civic participation.
